rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a pitchable inference and a landmine. A keeps the AI angle honest with "The two are supplied as separate facts; the link between them is unconfirmed," while B turns the same thin fact pattern into "Canva bought an AI image startup, then shipped it as a brand-safety feature." That is the kind of confident overreach that gets forwarded around a newsroom for the wrong reason.
gaps_in_A: "The launch is today, and it is the first product move that can be read against those two numbers" overclaims firstness. The update gives a launch, not Canva's full product history.

"Profitable and valued at $26B, Canva is now selling to the procurement office" is directionally plausible, but procurement is inferred from enterprise features. It needs actual buyer or sales-process proof.
"Why IT admins should care about Canva's single sign-on" — `duplicate` throws away a potentially useful CIO/identity-management angle. It is underproved, not automatically duplicative.
A underplays the sharpest weakness in the announcement: "named enterprise customers not disclosed." It asks the question, but B more correctly makes that absence central to the business-data angle.
gaps_in_B: "Canva bought an AI image startup, then shipped it as a brand-safety feature" invents the causal bridge. The update says recent acquisition plus AI tool; it does not say the acquired technology powers the enterprise generator.
"The acquisition and the AI generation feature land together" is not grounded. The update says the acquisition was recent, not that it landed with this launch.
"the exact moat Adobe has used to hold enterprise accounts" is unsupported competitive analysis. Good hunch, bad fact discipline.
"Canva can't name one enterprise customer" is stronger than the source allows. The announcement did not disclose named customers; that is not the same as Canva being unable to name one.
